questions.stem: What instrument is used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant?

options.text: Potometer
Thermometer
Voltmeter
Barometer

questions.explanation: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a plant shoot, which is closely related to the rate of transpiration. It tracks the movement of an air bubble along a capillary tube.

options.text: It tracks the movement of an air bubble in a water-filled tube as the plant takes up water
It measures the humidity around the plant
It weighs the amount of water lost
It measures the temperature of leaves

questions.explanation: A potometer has a graduated capillary tube connected to a plant shoot. As the plant takes up water, an air bubble moves along the tube, and the distance moved per unit time indicates the rate of uptake.

questions.stem: Why must the potometer be set up underwater?

options.text: To keep the plant cool
To dissolve minerals
To increase transpiration
To prevent air bubbles entering the system, which would block water flow

questions.explanation: The potometer must be assembled underwater to prevent air entering the system. Air bubbles in the xylem would break the continuous water column and prevent water transport.

questions.stem: What does a potometer actually measure?

options.text: The growth rate of the plant
The rate of water uptake, which is an estimate of transpiration rate
The rate of photosynthesis
Transpiration rate directly

questions.explanation: A potometer measures water uptake, not transpiration directly. Most water taken up is lost through transpiration, so uptake rate is a good estimate, though some water is used for photosynthesis and growth.

questions.stem: How could you use a potometer to investigate the effect of wind on transpiration?

options.text: Change the type of plant
Change the temperature of the water
Use a fan to create different wind speeds and measure the rate of bubble movement each time
Change the length of the tube

questions.explanation: Place a fan at different distances from the shoot to create different wind speeds, and measure how quickly the bubble moves each time. All other variables should be kept constant.

questions.stem: Why should you use the same plant and same sized leaves when comparing transpiration rates?

options.text: To use less water
To ensure a fair test by controlling variables that affect transpiration
To make the experiment look neat
To save time

questions.explanation: Using the same plant and similar leaf area ensures a fair test. Different plants or different leaf areas would introduce additional variables, making it impossible to determine the effect of the factor being tested.

questions.stem: Mass loss from a plant on a balance can also measure transpiration. Why?

options.text: The soil dries out
The plant gets heavier during transpiration
Carbon dioxide has mass
The mass lost is almost entirely due to water evaporating from the leaves

questions.explanation: Placing a plant (with the soil surface sealed) on a balance allows you to measure mass loss over time. Since the mass lost is almost entirely water vapour lost through transpiration, this gives a direct measure.
